prize_parts.citation: For the development of palladium-catalyzed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling
For the development of base editing, programmable chemical conversion of DNA bases without double-strand breaks

statement.case_for: Palladium-catalyzed C-N coupling is the clearest case on the shortlist of a general method that changed how chemists build bonds. Ligand design (bulky alkylphosphines and biaryl phosphines) took aryl amine synthesis from a harsh, substrate-limited exercise to a routine operation used daily in pharmaceutical and materials synthesis, and its adoption is visible in the literature and in industrial processes. The mechanism is well understood and the work has been confirmed for decades. Buchwald and Hartwig are the decisive pair. I pair it with David Liu's base editing as a second, distinct achievement because that is where the opening ballots show the broadest cross-member support (six of eight members rank B060), and because there is a chemical core to it: nucleobase deamination chemistry harnessed through protein evolution to give a programmable, single-nucleotide DNA transformation. That gives a prize with one traditional molecule-making achievement and one chemical-biology achievement, with only three names.
statement.case_against: Overlap with the 2010 cross-coupling prize may make C-N coupling look like an incremental extension of a recognised concept, and Kosugi's 1983 tin-amide precedent leaves a priority question. Base editing is young, its clinical record is short, it sits close to the 2020 CRISPR prize, and whether it is chemistry or biology is a fair question. Combining the two parts is a pragmatic coalition rather than a thematically unified prize, and it excludes Komor, Gaudelli, Kondo and Nishida from B060.

responses.point: Ranks C-N coupling first as a simple, broadly consequential method in the tradition of the 2010 prize, and notes that Kosugi's 1983 work has a real priority claim.
responses.response: I agree on the merit and on the Buchwald-Hartwig pair. On Kosugi I would qualify the priority point: the tin-amide chemistry needed stoichiometric tin and had narrow scope, so it was not a general catalytic method, and I would not give him a seat. Crediting him would also take the place needed for a second achievement. Your point about the 2010 overlap is a real objection, but the new chemistry here is C-N bond formation with amines, which differs from the earlier C-C couplings and required its own ligand generations.

responses.point: Proposes David Liu alone for base editing, with Komor and Gaudelli as decisive trainees, and asks whether it is distinct enough from the 2020 CRISPR prize.
responses.response: I agree that Liu alone is the cleaner configuration and I have followed it; crediting trainees is not usual committee practice. On distinctness from 2020, I think it is distinct: CRISPR-Cas9 makes double-strand breaks, while base editing is a chemical transformation of a nucleobase, which is what I look for when asking what was new chemically. I share your worry about Kondo and Nishida, whose Target-AID work was independent and contemporaneous, but I do not think it changes the single-laureate recommendation.

responses.point: Ranks nanopore sequencing first for a clear physical principle and a new capability in long-read, label-free sequencing, while acknowledging that the credit split among Deamer, Branton, Bayley and Akeson is a real problem.
responses.response: I accept the impact and that the principle is settled. My reservation is the one you raise: the original concept (Deamer and Branton), the engineered pore (Bayley) and the enzyme ratchet (Akeson) are three different contributions, and the configuration also depends on who among the credited names is living. For a chemistry prize I also ask what was new chemically, and much of the decisive step is engineering and instrumentation. I keep it as an alternative rather than a lead.

responses.point: Ranks biomolecular condensates first as physical chemistry at its core, a new organising principle for the cell, and accepts that in vivo rigour is still being sorted out.
responses.response: I respect the physical-chemistry framing, but I disagree on maturity. Several of you, including Andrei and Johan, note that the physiological relevance of many condensates is unresolved and that overexpression artefacts are common. A prize should honour a settled discovery, and I cannot name a chemical transformation or method in this field the way I can for the coupling or base editing. The exclusion of Pappu and Mittag also makes the three-person cut harder here than for the other candidates.

responses.point: Ranks targeted protein degradation first as a molecular design principle that redefines what is druggable, with an unresolved split between PROTAC and cereblon molecular-glue strands.
responses.response: I find it chemically interesting and keep it as an alternative. My concern is the one you list yourself: with no approved degrader drug, and the PROTAC and glue lines needing different laureates, it cannot yet be cleanly fitted into three names. If the committee prefers a medicinal-chemistry achievement over base editing as the second part, B041 is my fallback, but I would want approvals or a clearer allocation first.

uncertainties: How much weight to give Kosugi's 1983 precedent; I rely on recollection of the history, not verification.
Whether the committee regards C-N coupling as too close to the 2010 cross-coupling prize.
Whether base editing is too early and too close to the 2020 CRISPR prize, and whether Kondo and Nishida should share credit.
Whether colleagues who ranked B060 would accept it as the second part of a shared prize rather than alone.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile: it lists no mentor, collaborator or institutional tie to any shortlisted candidate. Pd-catalyzed coupling is close to my own field of synthetic methodology, which I note as a disciplinary bias rather than a personal tie.
